title: Lo, la, los, las
topic: direct object pronouns in the present tense
why: After gustar and its pronouns, this lesson introduces the direct object pronouns lo, la, los, las and me, te, nos, os, placed before the conjugated verb. They save you from repeating yourself in every everyday situation (shopping, lost items, invitations) and set up the unit review.

Lo, la, los, las: no more repeating

Like “it,” “him,” “her” and “them” in English, lo, la, los, las replace a direct object so you don't have to repeat it. They take the gender and number of the noun they replace. The big difference from English: there's no neutral “it.” Masculine and feminine things get different pronouns, and even “them” comes in a masculine and a feminine form.

Noun replacedPronounSpanishEnglish
masculine singularlo¿El pan? Lo compro yo.The bread? I'll buy it.
feminine singularla¿La tarta? La hace mi madre.The cake? My mother's making it.
masculine plurallos¿Los billetes? Los tiene Pablo.The tickets? Pablo has them.
feminine plurallas¿Las llaves? No las encuentro.The keys? I can't find them.

So you always need to know the gender of the Spanish noun: la tarta is feminine (the cake → la), el coche is masculine (the car → lo), even though both are just “it” in English.

Before the verb, not after

English puts “it” after the verb: “I open it,” “I'm waiting for her.” Spanish puts the pronoun in front: lo abro, la espero. Each pronoun is a separate, full word.

¿La ventana? Ahora la abro.The window? I'll open it right now.

Lo can also stand for a whole idea, where English often says nothing at all. It gives you the most useful phrases in the lesson: No lo sé (I don't know), Lo entiendo (I understand).

", "

Me, te, nos, os: when it's people

For people, you use the full set. Me, te, nos, os are the same as for the reflexive verbs you already know (me levanto, te duchas).

PronounEnglishSpanishEnglish
meme¿Me llamas mañana?Will you call me tomorrow?
teyouTe espero en la plaza.I'll wait for you in the square.
lo / lahim / her¿Conoces a Marta? — Sí, la conozco.Do you know Marta? — Yes, I know her.
nosusMis abuelos nos invitan a comer.My grandparents are inviting us to lunch.
osyou (plural)Chicos, os veo a las ocho.Guys, I'll see you at eight.
los / lasthemMis primos son simpáticos: los invito a cenar.My cousins are nice: I'm inviting them to dinner.

The personal a disappears when you use the pronoun: Conozco a Marta becomes La conozco.

Leísmo in Madrid

In Madrid and central Spain, you'll often hear le instead of lo for a man: ¿Conoces a Pablo? — Sí, le conozco. It's accepted for a male person. You just need to recognize it; you can say lo, which is correct everywhere.

Don't confuse this with the le of gustar (le gusta, he or she likes it). With gustar, the pronouns are le and les for everyone; for a direct object, a woman is always la: I see her, I know her.

", "

Where does the pronoun go?

This is the big difference from English: the pronoun goes right before the conjugated verb.

SentenceSpanishEnglish
StatementLo compro.I buy it.
NegativeNo lo compro.I don't buy it.
Question¿Lo compras?Do you buy it?
With a question word¿Dónde lo compras?Where do you buy it?

The no goes before the pronoun, never between the pronoun and the verb: No la conozco, not “la no conozco.”

And with an infinitive?

With querer, poder, tener que + infinitive, you'll hear two positions, both correct: Lo quiero comprar or Quiero comprarlo (attached to the end of the infinitive, no space). For now, just know that it exists; here we're practicing the pronoun before the conjugated verb.

¿Las gafas? Siempre las pierdo. ¿Y tú? ¿Dónde las pones?My glasses? I'm always losing them. What about you? Where do you put them?
¿Mi móvil? No lo encuentro. ¿Lo tienes tú?My phone? I can't find it. Do you have it?

To find the right pronoun, ask yourself two questions: is the noun masculine or feminine in Spanish? Singular or plural? Las llaves → las, el paraguas → lo, los regalos → los.
